colophon: Aṟputat Tiruvantāti, graciously composed by Karaikal Ammaiyar.

lines.1: Ever since I was born and learned to speak,
lines.2: my whole love has turned, excelling all else, to reach your radiant red feet alone —
lines.3: O Lord of the celestials, your throat dark and deep with the stain of poison,
lines.4: when will you put an end to this hardship of mine?
lines.5: Even if he does not lift away our troubles, even if he does not take pity on us,
lines.6: even if he does not grant the wide path of grace — still, toward him,
lines.7: our lord who dances in fire, blazing, decked always in bones,
lines.8: my heart's love will never fail.
lines.9: To him alone shall we belong, life after life, through seven births,
lines.10: to him alone shall our love be given, and to no other —
lines.11: for none but him wears the crescent, ever growing, in his matted hair;
lines.12: never, to any other, will our service go.
lines.13: We have become his servants; when we cried out our grief so he would know our suffering,
lines.14: why does he not hear it — this refusal to hear?
lines.15: He of the long and gracious form, his sacred throat turned another color,
lines.16: the lord who took us into his keeping.
lines.17: It is the Lord who brings every living being into existence;
lines.18: it is the Lord who, in time, brings about its passing;
lines.19: it is the Lord who, when we cry out to him, 'O Father,' in anguish,
lines.20: turns away the fierce sorrow that comes upon us.
lines.21: Let those who wish to call him 'the one of heaven' do so;
lines.22: let those who wish to call him 'the king of the gods in his own abode' do so —
lines.23: he who is knowledge itself, his throat dense with light yet darkened once by poison,
lines.24: I will only say: he dwells in my heart.
lines.25: I alone am blessed with true penance; my heart, truly, is a good heart;
lines.26: I alone have set my mind on ending birth itself;
lines.27: I alone have become the servant of the lord with the eye set in his forehead,
lines.28: wrapped in the elephant's hide, smeared white with ash.
lines.29: That day I became his — became the servant of one who is so rarely attained;
lines.30: is that not exactly how it came about?
lines.31: By the grace of him who bears the pure Ganga on his head, who is like a mountain of gold,
lines.32: who holds fire in his palm.
lines.33: It is grace alone by which the Lord governs every world;
lines.34: it is grace alone that cuts the bond of birth;
lines.35: by grace alone I am destined to look upon the true reality —
lines.36: grace, for me, is everything, always.
lines.37: My own sweet lord, my god — I have always held him
lines.38: as the dear treasure hidden in my heart;
lines.39: I have taken him as my lord, and in that alone I have found joy —
lines.40: is there anything left, then, that is hard for me to attain?
lines.41: One thing alone I have kept in my thoughts, one thing alone I have resolved upon,
lines.42: one thing alone I have locked within my heart — that one thing, see,
lines.43: is to belong to him who bears the Ganga and the radiant crescent in his crown,
lines.44: whose hand shines with gathered light.
lines.45: That alone is how he becomes our lord, that alone is how he takes us into his keeping —
lines.46: this, sweetly, we have come to understand;
lines.47: that alone, too, is the graciousness with which he set a single, matchless eye
lines.48: above the bright brow of her whose eyes are cool as dew.
lines.49: If he who is so gracious truly exists, it is unseemly, see,
lines.50: to let this fearsome thing draw near his broad chest —
lines.51: for should that great coiling serpent, drawing tighter,
lines.52: one day come close to the mountain's daughter, that would be a grievous wrong.
lines.53: My own solitary heart, by itself, will carry itself to safety,
lines.54: by itself will bring about its own great good,
lines.55: simply by holding in thought him who wears, gleaming on his chest as an ornament,
lines.56: the great serpent that spits venom like leaping flame.
lines.57: Even the gods, who adorn his feet with flowers and dwell in constant thought of him,
lines.58: do not thereby reach oneness with those sacred feet —
lines.59: so when I, who only cry out, 'O red matted-haired one, O holy Brahmin,'
lines.60: call to him now, what indeed will he do for me?
lines.61: Now indeed we are saved — we have reached the Lord's feet;
lines.62: now, O heart, no more troubles remain for us;
lines.63: now we have crossed the roaring ocean of unending birth,
lines.64: the very sea that our karma stirred up, see.
lines.65: He is of such a nature that he can be seen by those who truly look for him —
lines.66: seen by those who worship with joined hands, seen by those who look on him in love;
lines.67: to such seekers he appears as pure light within their own minds,
lines.68: Hara, who stands as the first cause of this ancient world.
lines.69: Shall I call him Hara? Shall I call him the four-faced Brahma?
lines.70: Shall I call him the rare, supreme being? I cannot truly grasp his nature —
lines.71: he who crushed the demon's pride beneath a single toe of his foot,
lines.72: he who has become everything, my own lord, this very day.
lines.73: Today, for us, it is easy — the wisdom to see him
lines.74: who was, even then, beyond the measure of Vishnu and four-faced Brahma;
lines.75: him who wears forever the crescent moon that never ages,
lines.76: him who becomes all twenty-one worlds.
lines.77: He himself is the one who knows, he himself is the one who makes known;
lines.78: he himself, as knowledge itself, is the knowing;
lines.79: he himself is the true reality that is known — the spreading sun, the earth, the sky —
lines.80: he himself is all of that.
lines.81: He alone becomes the sun and moon, the fire, and the open sky;
lines.82: he alone becomes the earth, the water, and the wind;
lines.83: he alone, having come among us, stands as the lord of the eight forms,
lines.84: the very embodiment of knowledge itself.
lines.85: Look closely and see through the intent of this sharp, venomous snake that has come —
lines.86: it means to seize the very thing it has come for;
lines.87: O you whose throat has darkened like the night itself, our lord,
lines.88: it is the crescent resting on your head that it means to take.
lines.89: Even if he shows us no pity — our lord who wears the crescent, the flood, the fire, and the serpent —
lines.90: still my heart will go on saying, again and again,
lines.91: 'we have become the servants of our father, whose throat bears the dark stain':
lines.92: this alone is what my heart holds.
lines.93: Is this not, then, the very form the Lord's grace takes?
lines.94: Is this not, then, my one true refuge?
lines.95: Is this not the very one — you who came back into my thought
lines.96: as a shining, lightning-bright form, and even now still circles here?
lines.97: What is the use of sitting here and asking why our lord,
lines.98: without a thought for himself, wanders everywhere begging in every guise,
lines.99: and why, in the depths of night, he dances in the burning-ground —
lines.100: we will find that reason only on the day we come to see him.
lines.101: His drooping, curling locks of matted hair flash like lightning on a mountain of gold;
lines.102: on the golden chest of him whose throat bears the dark stain,
lines.103: the serpent he has set there, amid the garland of bones,
lines.104: shows everywhere, glittering and shining bright.
lines.105: Do not, out of fondness, wear the serpent as an ornament on your chest —
lines.106: for many days now we have praised you, worshipped you, and begged you this,
lines.107: O you who broke your enemies' pride and burned their three cities with a single arrow;
lines.108: wear some other ornament instead, one of gold.
lines.109: Wearing one serpent as an ornament, fastening another as a fine, gleaming cord
lines.110: over his surging tiger-skin, and coiling yet another
lines.111: upon his golden crown — all this he wears;
lines.112: what, then, will become of me, who has no wisdom of my own?
lines.113: All those who cannot grasp his true meaning
lines.115: others merely see the guise of a ghost: a body red as flowers, smeared with ash
lines.116: and hung about with bones — that alone is what they see.
lines.117: He himself is the greatness that others cannot fathom;
lines.118: he himself is also the great awareness by which others come to know him —
lines.119: our lord, wearing the bones of others, dancing in fire through the night,
lines.120: rejoices there together with the fierce ghosts who attend him.
lines.121: Rejoice, O simple heart — among all humankind you too will shine,
lines.122: for you have found this great good fortune;
lines.123: and without scorn, let it grow ever greater — this deep love of yours
lines.124: for one who wanders wearing bones, whoever's bones they were.
lines.125: On his richly radiant, red matted hair it seems as though
lines.126: a single ray had come streaming down from the young crescent moon —
lines.127: but look closely: it is the sacred thread across the chest of him, the first of all eyes,
lines.128: the ever-youthful eye in his forehead, who long ago burned down the three cities.
lines.129: Let those who merely talk book-learning, without ever entering its truth, wander as they will —
lines.130: such is the very nature of him whose throat is dark as a precious sapphire:
lines.131: to whoever performs whatever penance, seeking whatever form of him,
lines.132: he becomes, exactly in that guise, that very form.
lines.133: Fierce karma cannot help but find its own way to those who need it —
lines.134: just as the three cities in the sky, who would not call themselves his servants,
lines.135: were burned away by a single arrow, so too will karma strike down
lines.136: all who fail to hold him close within their hearts.
lines.137: See how it looks — as though the darkness itself, fearing the white moon,
lines.138: had come and taken refuge in its own place;
lines.139: that is what the dark mark looks like on the fair, sapphire throat
lines.140: of him who wears the hooded, wide-mouthed serpent fastened there.
lines.141: O you whose throat bears the dark mark — see how the serpent on your long, flowing hair
lines.142: wanders about wasting away, afraid it will be crushed;
lines.143: and if, eager for it, that serpent should come racing over the crescent,
lines.144: would the young moon, in such fear, ever grow to fullness?
lines.145: He who destroyed the three great fortress-cities of the mighty demons who refused to honor him,
lines.146: he in whose ever-growing matted hair the moon makes its home —
lines.147: if, with true understanding, one praises him rather than scorning his body hung with bones,
lines.148: then never again in this world will that one be born into a body of bones.
lines.149: Just as the moon, rising bright into the sky, shrinks small
lines.150: the moment the gleaming serpent touches it —
lines.151: so too, on the chest of him who wears the serpent as a garland,
lines.152: the sharp, dark tusk of the wild boar flourishes and gleams.
lines.153: The lovely, coral-red form of the graceful lord who holds, on one side of himself,
lines.154: a slender flowering branch — that form, before,
lines.155: resembled a fine mountain of red gold; when it is covered with sacred ash,
lines.156: it resembles instead a jeweled mountain of silver.
lines.157: Turn back, O simple heart, and with your own mouth
lines.158: speak of, and worship with true intent, the feet of his devotees;
lines.159: and keep away from the company of those who hold no true regard
lines.160: for him who wears, as a small garland, the crescent moon no other has ever worn.
lines.161: If, on one side of you, is Vishnu who once measured out the worlds,
lines.162: and on the other side is Uma herself —
lines.163: then, both sides being your own form, we can no longer tell which hue is truly yours:
lines.164: is this your own form, or hers, joined together like lightning?
lines.165: Did it shrink small only to suit the serpent,
lines.166: or did you yourself cut it down to size and set it fittingly there?
lines.167: Or is it simply that this infant moon cannot, in time,
lines.168: grow the way a mother nurses her child to flourish? Tell me, why is this so?
lines.169: 'Wearing this crescent, do not wander the streets for meager alms' —
lines.170: even if we beg you this, our great lord,
lines.171: if the radiant gods themselves cannot hold you back, how could we?
lines.172: He alone truly knows what is right for himself.
lines.173: Why is it that he does not grant his grace to me,
lines.174: who lives only as his servant, having taken refuge in him alone —
lines.175: he, the glorious one, so sweet to the heart, the bridegroom of Ganga,
lines.176: of ruddy form and great renown, the lord of the celestials?
lines.177: Cherishing only the great path that leads toward the Lord,
lines.178: seeking only the Lord's own great grace —
lines.179: if you ask, 'where has the Lord gone?', know that he dwells
lines.180: even within the thoughts of ones like me; to those who truly look, he is easy to find, right here.
lines.181: Is this not, in truth, an easy thing — O you poor, pitiable, unknowing ones, alas —
lines.182: this way of living with the mind fixed
lines.183: truly and inwardly on our lord, our own father,
lines.184: whose throat shines dark, as he wanders freely?
lines.185: O simple heart, apart from going to him and reaching him through devotion,
lines.186: is there any other way to attain him at all, you fool?
lines.187: The good fortune of reaching those sacred feet comes only through the grace
lines.188: of him who gave half of himself to her of the lovely, dark feet.
lines.189: The great lord watches the fine tusk of the boar upon his sacred chest,
lines.190: and gazes too at the tender young crescent —
lines.191: and the serpent, to this very day, has never once discerned
lines.192: which of the two is truly the moon; it has no wisdom of its own.
lines.193: That fine young crescent, curved as if shaped and polished smooth,
lines.194: runs its course, its mingled rays spreading wide —
lines.195: and so his matted locks, which have no equal but himself,
lines.196: come to look as though gold and silver had been twisted together as one.
lines.197: It looks as though the fruit of the konrai tree on his matted hair
lines.198: had come forth and hung down along his side —
lines.199: such is the dark, cloud-blue hair of the noble lady who forms one half
lines.200: of him who wears the fair crescent on the right side of his crown.
lines.201: Do not go forth, taking with you as your beautiful other half
lines.202: her of the fine, dark hair and bright bangles,
lines.203: to that place where, your anklets ringing, in the depth of night,
lines.204: amid the roaring fire, you dance in the great burning-ground with the ghosts.
lines.205: Even if countless full moons should rise together, sweetly,
lines.206: filling the whole wide, sunset-red sky, it could not equal
lines.207: the splendor with which the garland of skulls appears,
lines.208: worn on the red matted hair of him who holds red-eyed Vishnu as one part of himself.
lines.209: With the glorious konrai in full bloom, and the great river's waters,
lines.210: roaming far and flooding rich upon it,
lines.211: and the famed serpent tied fast as its cord — the golden crown of our lord
lines.212: appears, to those who behold it, exactly like a fresh rain-cloud.
lines.213: O our lord whose throat is dark as a cloud, the eye of our brow —
lines.214: where were you hidden, that he who wanders as one being with you,
lines.215: whose very body seems fashioned from a water-laden cloud,
lines.216: went unseen, long ago, even by the one who is your own other half?
lines.217: Not only did his throat darken long ago, when he drank the poison
lines.218: of the churned ocean, making the very gods tremble —
lines.219: that same scar shows too, upon his red matted hair,
lines.220: within the milk-white moon, as the dark mark on that precious jewel.
lines.221: If you truly hold it to be no blemish, then tell us this,
lines.222: O you whose hue is the burning white ash —
lines.223: we have heard it said, spoken openly, that you eat your food
lines.224: from a raw, white skull, you who wear the moonlight itself upon your head.
lines.225: Even if you must go begging through the whole world,
lines.226: go, see, but leave that fierce serpent of yours behind —
lines.227: for innocent women, frightened by the venomous snake
lines.228: dancing wildly upon you, will never dare come near to give you alms.
lines.229: Even setting side by side the two most matched of things could never equal it —
lines.230: not blazing fire and thick, gathering darkness together;
lines.231: for on his chest, his own red matted hair, and there, upon his golden form,
lines.232: the flower-decked hair of she who is his other half — such is his glory.
lines.233: I am unable to grasp your true nature; you yourself must tell me and show me,
lines.234: O you whose forehead holds an eye, whose throat bears the dark stain —
lines.235: is the sacred ash you wear upon that half joined to the woman,
lines.236: or upon the half joined to Vishnu? On which side does it lie, on your two-fold form?
lines.237: Even if towering clouds should gather and, like a golden mountain,
lines.238: blot out its whole radiance, that still could not equal
lines.239: the sight, long ago, when our lord's own sacred body
lines.240: was wrapped in the dark hide of that raging, rutting elephant.
lines.241: Without ever having seen his sacred form, I became his servant on that very day;
lines.242: and even today, still, I have not seen that sacred form —
lines.243: so what am I to say to those who ask me, 'what form does your Lord take?'
lines.244: What form is it indeed — what, truly, is your form?
lines.245: What resembles it, what does not, what it becomes and what it does not —
lines.246: who can ever truly know the answer to that?
lines.247: On the day you took the form of a hunter armed with a bow
lines.248: and contended with Arjuna, what was that fierce hunter's form truly like?
lines.249: Does the moonlight on your crown, rivaling the shapely red sun itself,
lines.250: wander abroad and go on blazing through the whole long day?
lines.251: O radiant one whose glory can never be told to its end,
lines.252: tell us this, we beg you.
lines.253: Does it roam and wander about, as though it means to seize
lines.254: the moonlit, white crescent for itself? —
lines.255: his sacred crown looks exactly like the red evening sky where the moon still lingers,
lines.256: and the serpent coiled within it, exactly like the break of dawn.
lines.257: His body shines like the very break of dawn;
lines.258: the white ash upon it shines like the fierce heat of open noon;
lines.259: the mass of his matted hair takes on the very shape of evening twilight;
lines.260: and his throat is like the swelling darkness of deepest night.
lines.261: O you who hold the poison within your own throat —
lines.262: did the serpent that dances, its hood spread wide, upon your chest,
lines.263: come by its own dark throat from licking at yours and taking the poison?
lines.264: Or is that ink-black hue simply its own, dark as gathered night?
lines.265: Because the serpent, the moon, the gentle deer, and the leaping tiger
lines.266: all hang together in their proper places, like a falling stream —
lines.267: it is fitting indeed that the anklet should rest
lines.268: upon the beautiful, sacred foot of him, golden-formed, the radiant eye set in his brow.
lines.269: Wishing to soothe away her sulking, she whose feet wear anklets,
lines.270: he pressed his own red-dyed feet against hers —
lines.271: and so, gaining that fresh beauty, the crown of him who wears the ever-young crescent
lines.272: came to outshine even the facing evening sky in just this splendor.
lines.273: We have been blessed to celebrate, bowing low upon this earth,
lines.274: our great and fitting servitude to him, the three-eyed one,
lines.275: who bears the curved crescent on his crown, who crushed cruel Death
lines.276: beneath his own good foot — is there any hardship left for us now?
lines.277: Is this, then, our great longing, never to be stilled —
lines.278: will you, O father, one day show us that place,
lines.279: O you whose twisted, matted hair is like leaping flame,
lines.280: where in the depths of night, holding fire, you dance amid the leaping flames?
lines.281: If you have set the moon that rises on your left side
lines.282: close beside some other, innocent young woman —
lines.283: know that we can see no trace at all of the mountain's daughter,
lines.284: who holds your left half as her own; look and see this yourself, O three-eyed one.
lines.285: If I cannot see you, bow to you as 'my own father,'
lines.286: and serve you with these very hands, then even if I were given the whole universe,
lines.287: I would not want it — O you who, as the crescent ruling the sky,
lines.288: are the very eye of all the seven great worlds, this alone is my resolve.
lines.289: Whatever your heart truly sets its intent upon, all of it
lines.290: can at once be set right — this I say to you firmly:
lines.291: O my heart, desire only this, and forever recite
lines.292: the lotus feet of him who bore the swelling, flooding waters upon his head.
lines.293: They say that pouring in even all the vast, surging seas
lines.294: could never fill it at all —
lines.295: yet how strange, that his skull-bowl comes to brim full
lines.296: with the unthinking alms that simple women give, never knowing what it truly is.
lines.297: Because the swirling waters of the Ganga move within it,
lines.298: and because the shining moon travels across it,
lines.299: and because the serpent glides upon the tall crown of him of such gracious form —
lines.300: his spreading, matted hair, looked at closely, seems to be the very sky itself.
lines.301: As the fortunate celestials of the sky bow down,
lines.302: rubbing their fresh gold, jeweled crowns against them,
lines.303: until, everywhere, O father, they grow worn with scars —
lines.304: alas, what a grievous wrong this is, done to your feet that are like the lovely lotus!
lines.305: When he lifts his foot, the very netherworld trembles and shifts;
lines.306: when he moves his crown, the vast heavens themselves shift;
lines.307: when his bangled hand turns and dances, the directions of the sky shift —
lines.308: dance on, knowing this, though the very ground beneath cannot bear it.
lines.309: Will he who dances, seemingly for no reason, in the ghost-filled burning-ground as his own stage,
lines.310: ever show mercy to every humble, struggling life?
lines.311: If he should show that mercy, then to one who bows and pleads for many days,
lines.312: what would he not become, what world would he not grant in his compassion?
lines.313: Bowing down, adorning with flowers the feet of him of spreading matted hair,
lines.314: and praising those who so adorn him —
lines.315: resolved always to render service to our own father —
lines.316: is this, perhaps, the very pride that fills a devoted heart?
lines.317: However great the pride with which that strong-shouldered demon lifted the mountain,
lines.318: he stood before him and crushed it down;
lines.319: and the same foot whose glorious end Vishnu and Brahma could not find,
lines.320: crying out in wonder and joyful praise — that same foot conquered and kicked Death away.
lines.321: We have conquered Death himself; we have slipped free of fierce hell;
lines.322: we have cut off, at the very root, both our past and future karma —
lines.323: by taking refuge at the lotus feet of him who loosed the burning arrow
lines.324: that made his enemies' fair fortress wither and fall like a dying lotus.
lines.325: To those who turn away from him, his very hair is like a deadly vine of fire —
lines.326: though to those who draw near in love, that same hair turns gentle as gold —
lines.327: so says the lightning-bright lady, of the flame-hued one before whom
lines.328: even the setting sun's red rays must fade: his flowing, matted hair.
lines.329: If you ask what it looks like, to those who behold it,
lines.330: when he of lightning-bright, red matted hair stands joined together with Vishnu —
lines.331: it looks, at full height, exactly as though a mountain of gold,
lines.332: like himself, and a mountain of blue sapphire stood there together.
lines.333: One eye of his is like the fierce, blazing fire itself,
lines.334: the next like the cool-rayed moon, the third like the sun's harsh, burning light —
lines.335: and it was that same eye which watched, as the three cities of his enemies
lines.336: were destroyed and consumed in the burning fire — the eye of the three-eyed one.
lines.337: Beholding him to my heart's content with my own eyes, joining my hands in full worship,
lines.338: and turning him over in thought again and again without measure —
lines.339: will I truly come to rejoice, calling out always, 'O dancer in fire, O lord of the heavens,'
lines.340: if I am ever granted the sight of that great one?
lines.341: Even were we granted that, we would want nothing else besides;
lines.342: and even should it slip from us and never come again —
lines.343: having glimpsed even a little of his grace, we have become one
lines.344: among the blessed company of ghosts belonging to him who set a third eye upon his brow.
lines.345: If we take garlands of flowers and, in love, adorn
lines.346: the golden feet of our lord who wears the serpent as his garland,
lines.347: and hold fast to that one true wisdom alone — what, then, can stand in our way?
lines.348: That darkness we call karma striking us down will surely be dispelled.
lines.349: Shall I call it the very shape of darkness itself? Shall I call it a great, massed cloud?
lines.350: Shall I call it a bewildering, deep sapphire blue?
lines.351: O you who hold such good grace for us, who wear on your red matted hair
lines.352: the white moon, gleaming and clear — what, then, shall I call the color of your throat?
lines.353: You turned mighty Manmatha to lightless ash with a single glance,
lines.354: and you dwell always within the clear, discerning mind —
lines.355: yet the mouth that drank the gleaming poison remains just as it was;
lines.356: how is it, then, that your throat alone took on this darkness? Tell us.
lines.357: Tell us this, O father: the surging waves of the Ganga,
lines.358: dragging along with them both the fierce, gliding serpent and the white moon,
lines.359: roar and rush onward — and if they should rise higher still,
lines.360: overwhelming and undoing your own cool matted hair, what then would you do?
lines.361: Having become servants at the feet of him whose red matted hair holds the flowing river,
lines.362: and having joined ourselves to his sacred word, we have truly come to understand — see!
lines.363: know, then, that we are provided for in this life and the next, in every way;
lines.364: so why, then, do you speak ill of us behind our back?
lines.365: He who is the very treasure that grants grace to the celestials —
lines.366: he who owns me, he who stands alone, the one and only,
lines.367: he who, by his own nature, does not know his own greatness,
lines.368: he whose pure matted hair curls as though wrought of gold, set aside as the treasure of grace for the gods.
lines.369: He, see, is the one of lovely, coral-red hue; he, see, is —
lines.370: the one whose form is beyond all others, matchless among the gods —
lines.371: he whose throat holds the dark, settled stain: toward him alone, O good heart,
lines.372: truly settle your love, and desire him with all your heart.
lines.373: Is it out of love that you cannot bear to part from her?
lines.374: Or is it simply that you have no other place to dwell apart?
lines.375: O rider of the great bull, dark as a rain-cloud, tell us —
lines.376: does she, the mountain's daughter, fear to live apart from you? Tell us plainly.
lines.377: She, a woman of noble family, never once leaves your side;
lines.378: and this other, a daughter of the waters, is here beside you too —
lines.379: O you who wear the white ash and the bones, you have never known separation from either;
lines.380: so tell us, among these two, which one holds the greater love?
lines.381: So that only those capable of true devotion might ever see him,
lines.382: we have wrapped Hara in that very covering we call love,
lines.383: and, through the glorious kinship that is rightly ours,
lines.384: we have locked him fast within our own heart, hidden there by this very mystery.
lines.385: Have you hidden it away, kept safe within all seven worlds?
lines.386: Or have you, with such sure strength, taken it up and held it fast in your own forearm —
lines.387: that red, blazing fire which, rising in full force to consume the three worlds,
lines.388: you drew up from within them and now carry away?
lines.389: Did your palm turn red from the fire that dances within it?
lines.390: Or did the fire itself turn red, simply from the beauty of your palm —
lines.391: as, your anklets ringing, in the forest where the ghosts dance,
lines.392: you hold flame aloft, shining bright, and dance in fire? Tell us this.
lines.393: Is it for her of the young, firm breasts to behold,
lines.394: or is it for that very host of ghosts in the fiery burning-ground to see,
lines.395: that you dance? Tell us plainly, O you who wear upon your chest
lines.396: the five-headed serpent whose gaping mouths spit flame — for whose sake is this dance of yours?
lines.397: When it walks, the earth trembles; when it looks, the very directions blaze;
lines.398: when it roars, the whole world groans aloud —
lines.399: O golden one, is this mount of yours a lion wrestling the mountains, a creature of the heavens,
lines.400: truly a bull, or the thunderbolt itself? Tell us this plainly, as one single truth.
lines.401: Those who devotedly recite this garland of antati verses,
lines.402: these words spoken by the Pey of Karaikkal that dissolve sorrow in the telling,
lines.403: those who go forth and praise the Lord with love that is never satisfied,
lines.404: will be born into a love that never departs, that never fades.
